messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Self-Consciousness: Being seen, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

It was a Tuesday afternoon in late October when a convoy of black SUVs rolled past the ranger station where Dev worked, and the sight of them—the clean, dark vehicles, the suggestion of uniforms inside—sent him straight back to the room. He had been held for eleven days in that concrete cell, blindfolded for most of it, fed only when his captors remembered. The men who kept him had worn uniforms too, though never insignia he could identify. They had asked questions he could not answer, and when he could not answer, they had broken his ribs and his left hand. Now, years later, a line of cars on a park road could make him feel the ache in those bones again, could make him see the bare bulb swinging overhead, the chipped paint on the wall, the way the light fell across the floor in exactly three slivers. He had come to believe that the sight of a uniform, or even talk of the military on the radio, meant that what happened to him was still happening—that he was still the kind of person who got trapped and broken. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, he was certain. Somebody else would have seen it coming.

The memory did not arrive as a story. It arrived as a series of frozen images: the door closing, the first blow, the taste of blood, the silence afterward. Sometimes he could recall these moments and feel nothing at all, as if he were watching a stranger on a screen. But more often, when the memory came, so did the pain. His ribs would ache. His left hand would cramp. And he would feel again the humiliation of begging, of being stripped, of being seen at his most helpless. That feeling of being seen—of being exposed—had not left him. He had become hyperaware of his own visibility. On the trail, when hikers glanced his way, he felt certain they could tell. They could see the weakness in him, the thing that had happened, the stain of it. He started to avoid the busier sections of the park, volunteering instead for the backcountry patrols where he might go hours without encountering anyone. When he did run into visitors, he found himself agreeing with whatever they said—yes, the trail is that way, yes, the weather will hold—even when he knew they were wrong. It was easier to please them, to disappear into their approval, than to risk being seen as difficult or defiant. He had learned that defiance got you hurt.

At night, alone in his cabin, the images came back unbidden. A glimpse of a uniform on a television show. The crackle of a radio. The sudden movement of a deer bursting from the brush. That last one was the worst. Any unexpected motion near him—a bird taking flight, a branch falling—and he would flinch, his heart hammering, his body bracing for a blow that was not coming. Even when he told himself he was safe, even when the forest was quiet and the stars were out, he could not make himself believe it. The world felt dangerous in a way that reason could not touch. He found himself controlling what little he could: his food. He began to restrict his eating, carefully measuring portions, skipping meals, because the discipline of hunger made him feel less helpless. It was something he could decide. It was something that belonged to him.

The revenge fantasies came less often now, but they still surfaced. He would imagine finding the men who had held him, making them feel what he had felt. But the fantasies did not comfort him. They only made him feel more isolated, more set apart from the ordinary life he saw other people living. His partner, Priya, did not understand why he flinched when she touched him from behind, or why he had stopped going to the grocery store when it was busy. She asked him what was wrong, and he told her nothing. He had learned that telling the truth did not help. It only made people look at you differently. And being looked at—being seen—was the thing he feared most.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning in the park when a school group arrived, and one of the children wore a small camouflage hat. Dev saw the hat and froze. The images came: the blindfold, the pain, the humiliation. He excused himself to the restroom and did not come out for twenty minutes. That evening, he called Priya and told her he needed help. He was afraid that if he did not, he would lose the job he loved, the relationship he was barely holding together, and the last thread of himself. He was hoping, though he could not yet say it aloud, that someone might finally show him how to stop seeing the room every time he opened his eyes.
